chapter_theme: More songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 2 of 6): the poet confesses to deceitful women who call wealthy men home, to eyes as deadly as the churned poison, and to a body bent by age and bound for hell; he pictures Yama coming while wife, sons and kin weep, asks for the silent seal the sects cannot know, and in three songs speaks for a girl sick with love. The praise names the Goddess in long litanies, Unnamulai of Arunai, Siva who could not be found by Vishnu and Brahma, and Murugan who hid his form to follow Valli.
structure_note: Women and their deceits (383 to 387, 391 to 393, 395), with 386 and 387 on women's eyes as poison; death and Yama (388, 389, 392); the silent seal and the sects (394); and the akam laments of a lovesick girl (390, 396, 397). 384 and 386 to 390 share closing formulas (அரியர பிரம புரந்தராதியர் தம்பிரானே; அரிவையும் ஒருபங்கு இடமுடையவர்).

383.reading: The poet asks that, seeing the throngs of deceitful, quarrelsome, tricky women, he not fall into the folly of delusion nor tend this divided body, but that birth, change and death leave him and he think in his mind of Murugan's sharp vel, his cock and the hunter girl of the millet slope. The praise names Kandavel of Arunai's street, the vel that went to free the gods' prisoners in the old sky, the lord who saw the world live when Sura and his foot soldiers fell, and the comrade-lord of those who sing scattering flowers of knowledge on his feet.
383.nuance: சாதக விகாரச் சாதல் may be birth (ஜாதகம்), change and death, the bodily cycle. The remedy is contemplation of the Lord's emblems (vel, cock, Valli) rather than his feet. The opening (பேதக விரோதத் தோதக விநோத) and the line ending தென்படாதே are hard to divide.

384.reading: The poet asks for grace not to fall into the maya of the sweet-tongued women who say to men of wealth 'by my oath, by your oath, my house is near, come there', foolish, quarrelsome and wicked, sauntering in the streets. The praise is a long litany of the Goddess, Kumari, Kali, Varahi, Maheswari, Gauri, Mahamayi, Abhirami, Narayani, sister of Vishnu, she who drank the poison of the sea, mother Uma who became all the Vedas, and names Murugan her son, whose vel fed the ghouls on the asuras' heads, roaming on the cloud-touched tower of Sonesar's Annamalai.
384.nuance: பொருளுளாரை, men of wealth, names whom the women call: the invitation 'my house is near' is the courtesan's speech of 21. The praise is chiefly of the Goddess, gathering the names of fierce and gentle forms (Kali, Varahi, Kapali, Abhirami) into the one mother Uma. Some names in the litany (மோடி, நிராபரி, சுடாரணி) are uncertain to me.

385.reading: The poet speaks of women who melt men like wax, comb their long hair on the street platforms, cover and loosen their breasts with their garments, play tricks and talk with deceitful hearts, and calls himself the great sinner and dunce who has fallen into their long net in the sea of strife and does not know love; he asks the sea of compassion, husband of two consorts, to give him his feet and rule him. The praise names Brahma and the gods who praise him, Vishnu with the tulasi garland as uncle, the bright vel, the one who circles the seven worlds, son of the Lady whom Hara embraces, at Arunai with its golden tower, walls and streets.
385.nuance: நேசமது அறியாத கசட மூடன்: the poet's fault is that he does not know love, set against the women's false love. The praise's உலகேழ் வலம் வருவோனே recalls the circling of the world in the contest for the fruit.

386.reading: The poet likens women's eyes to the dark poison of Siva's throat and to Murugan's own vel, Siva being described in full with hide, serpent, crescent, Ganga, fire, axe and deer, the burner of Kama; these eyes press against the earrings and swallow the lives of men like Kama, and he asks whether his dying, body and mind ruined in their embrace, will not end. The praise pictures asura heads falling like broken Meru while ghouls walk as at an offering, Kumara in Arunai's tall tower, and the one who left the six-faced form the Vedas praise to go among hunters and embrace the forest girl, lord of Hari, Hara, Brahma and Indra.
386.nuance: The simile is bold: the eyes that kill are compared to the poison Siva holds in his throat (கண்டகாளம்) and to the vel Murugan loves (உனது உள் உகந்த வேல்), so the deadly look is matched with the Lord's own weapons. அறுமுக வடிவை ஒழிந்து: Murugan put aside his six-faced form for Valli, a theme repeated in 387.

387.reading: The poet compares women's eyes to the poison that rose when the gods churned the sea with Meru as post and the serpent king as rope, a poison that spread like massed clouds, shook the elephants and mountains of the eight directions and cracked the cosmic egg; these eye-nets, guilty of the five great sins, take lovers' lives as sacrifice, and he asks whether love for such women will not end. The praise shows Taraka destroyed and the gods restored, Murugan son of Unnamulai, the ever-new goddess of Arunai, who in great infatuation hid his form and followed a hunter girl through the forest.
387.nuance: The churning of the sea is told in full only to explain a simile: the women's eyes are that poison. அருந்துணாமுலை (உண்ணாமுலை) is the name of the Goddess at Thiruvannamalai; the song names her as Murugan's mother. அடவியில் வடிவு கரந்து போய் ஒரு குறமகள் பிறகு திரிந்த காமுக: the god himself is called the lover (காமுக) who trailed the hunter girl, a playful answer to the poet's own desire.

388.reading: The poet asks that, before Yama with charred form and fiery eyes comes for his life while his wife and fine sons stand weeping and telling their griefs, Murugan look on him so that through knowledge his troubles leave and he can think of the two feet. The praise names the vel that cut the shoulders of Sura, at whose coming Vishnu, Brahma and the eight directions trembled, and Arunai of Siva, who for the Vedic priests, the gods and his devotees gave a share of himself to the Lady who practised dharma.
388.nuance: அறம் மேவும் அரிவையும் ஒருபங்கு இடமுடையவர்: Siva sharing his body with the Lady who practised dharma, perhaps pointing to Arunai's story that Uma there gained half of Siva; the song does not tell it. The meaning of the opening (இரவியும் மதியும் தெரிவுற எழும் அம்புவி தனில் இனம் ஒன்றிடு மாது) is uncertain.

389.reading: The poet pictures Yama coming by fate's way with cunning, crushing trouble and cruel disease, eyes like hot fire, raging that today is the day to take the life, while women and kin, their hearts surging, pour tears; before that tumult comes, he asks for the nature to worship the feet that remove the deeds of the line. The praise names Vishnu on the serpent and Brahma of the old Vedas, and Siva who drank the poison to end the gods' fear, rides the bull, wears the snake, moon and Ganga in his hair and fire in his hand, and shares himself with the Lady, at whose Arunai Murugan dwells.
389.nuance: விதி வழி வந்திடு போதில்: Death comes along fate's path. குல வினை களையும் கழல், feet that clear the deeds of the line, may mean inherited karma or the deeds that make up birth. The praise is entirely of Siva; Murugan appears only in the closing பெருமாளே.

390.reading: A lament for a lovesick girl, in the voice of one who watches her: should the girl, her bangles slipping in her infatuation, suffer on her lone flower bed, harried by the moon rising from the sea of sharks and makaras, by the small south breeze that comes like fire through the street where two-faced women live, and by the arrows of the bodiless god? The praise names the vel that scattered the asuras' crowns, the chest wedded to the hunter girl, the lord on the peacock at Arunai, and the master of Hari, Hara and Brahma whom the Vedas declare.
390.nuance: சரிவளை கழல, bangles slipping, is the classical sign of wasting in love. இருவினை மகளிர் மருவிய தெருவு, the street where women of double dealing live, seems to be the gossips of the town; the phrase could instead name courtesans.

391.reading: The poet asks whether, melting under women of elephant gait, by ruinous deeds that bring distress, never thinking of salvation, not knowing praise and sunk in ruinous pleasure, he must wear himself out in the world with this body of flesh and blame; he asks to enter the shade of the tree that is Murugan's feet, a raft of lotus. The praise names him the one who imprisoned Brahma, nephew of Vishnu, Murugan of Tripurai, in whom the burner of the cities delights, the vel that split the demons' hill, at Arunai, famous shrine, by the north side of its long wall.
391.nuance: சததள மலர்வார் புணை நின கழல் ஆர் தருநிழல்: the feet are both a raft and the shade of a tree, two images of refuge in one line (as in 377). வடசார், the north side of the wall, may place this song at a shrine within the temple.

392.reading: The poet asks not to droop clinging in desire to those who twist the good, not to perish crushed beneath mighty Death's foot, and not to be born into the sea of misery by cultivating friendship with the wicked, but to be given the holy feet and told the teaching of the arts. The praise names Murugan who dwells in the minds of those who think of him once and say his name twice, the victor who hid the hunter girl's honey on his chest and ran off, and the vel that fought proud Sura, at the holy tower on the red hill.
392.nuance: கருக்காரர் நட்பை பெருக்கு ஆசரித்து, cultivating the friendship of wicked men, adds bad company to women and death. ஒருக்கால் நினைத்திட்டு இருக்கால் மிகுத்திட்டு உரைப்பார்: devotion asks little, one thought and two utterances. ஒளித்தோடும், running away in hiding with Valli, is the eloping lover. The opening phrase அருக்கு ஆர் நலத்தைத் திரிப்பார் is hard to construe.

393.reading: The poet traces a life spent leaning on the breasts of carp-eyed women never parted from Kama, until strength fails, the body bends, he walks coughing, speech goes, feeling ends and the life grows faint, and asks for Murugan's two feet so that he does not enter fire-mouthed hell. The praise names the vel that ground the great hill to dust, the twelve golden shoulders that melted for the hunter girl, the one dear to Hara whom Vishnu and Brahma could not discern with their eyes, at the holy street of Arunapuri among rich fields.
393.nuance: The plea runs as one life, lust then decay (இருமா நடைபுக்கு, walking with a cough) then hell. திருமால் கமலப் பிரமா விழியின் தெரியா அரன், Hara whom Vishnu and lotus Brahma could not see, is the story of the column of fire that Thiruvannamalai claims as its own.

394.reading: The poet, crying 'come, come', worshipping, melting and losing himself in the sea of love, seeks the seal of silence that the great sinners of the noisy sects cannot know, and asks whether, without gaining the flawless true reality of jnana, he must fall into the whirlpool of the sea of birth, a mere bubble. The praise names Murugan the child of the six who drank their breasts on the bank of the old Ganga, the skilled one on the peacock at the red hill, whose vel made the fish-filled sea and the Vedas alike cry 'ko ko'.
394.nuance: மோன முத்திரை, the seal of silence, is set against the கோலாகலச் சமயம், the uproar of the sects, as in 369. புற்புதமாய பிறவி வாராகரச் சுழி: birth is a bubble in a whirlpool of the sea. The opening line has a garbled word (தொழுத்மு டூடு).

395.reading: The poet speaks of women with heavy breasts and flowered hair who hide in their garments, talk and laugh, bewitch anyone for the love of wealth, send messengers by hand and snatch a man's money, and asks for Murugan's feet of light for himself, who burns on the way to the seven hells through their tricks. The praise sounds the drums of the battle in which Sura was slain, names Murugan son of the one who dances with a raised foot, the vel that melted at the hunter girl's breasts, and the lord gracious to both the peacock of the field and the gods' true daughter at Arunai's tower.
395.nuance: ஆசை பொருட்டு, for the desire of wealth, and கைத் தூதுவிடுத்தே பொருளைப் பறி, sending go-betweens and snatching money, name the trade. சோதி ஒளிப் பாதம், feet of light, may glance at the hill of fire. The opening simile (ஆனை வரிக் கோடு) is unclear.

396.reading: In the voice of a lovesick woman alone on her flower bed: tormented by Kama's cruel arrows and the small breeze of the end, by the great moon that bears the hare and sets her body on fire, and by the sea that sends its waves to the shore, she asks whether it is fitting that her life droop, and whether her grief will not end. The praise names the vel thrown at Sura on golden Meru, the hero who came to the millet field to delight the hunter girl, dwelling in Arunai's street among screwpine-hedged fields, king of the unblinking gods.
396.nuance: The torments are the classical three of akam night, the wind, the moon and the sea, each given its own line ending in -ஆலே. இறுதிச் சிறுகால், the small wind of the end, makes the breeze a herald of death. The closing அவனித் திருமாதொடு சிவனுக்கு is hard to construe.

397.reading: A short lament for a lovesick girl, spoken for her: by the moon, the king of cold, that strikes fire, by the young north wind and the town that reproaches her, and by the arrows Kama takes up for war, the lone doe's life faints; grant her a word of grace. The praise names Kumara, Muruga, guru of the matted-haired Siva, the chest that quenches the hunter girl's desire, the giver of Amaravati back to the gods, standing in the street of Arunapuri.
397.nuance: இளவாடையும் ஊரும் ஒறுக்கும்: the north wind and the town punish her together, gossip set beside the weather. தனிமான், the lone doe, is the girl spoken of in third person, so the voice is a mother or friend.

links.note: Both quote the courtesan's invitation, 'come to my house' (21's இங்கு நின்றது என் வீடே, 384's அருகு வீடு இதுதான் அதில் வாரும்); 384 adds that it is spoken to men of wealth and sworn on oaths.

Both give a woman's eyes the power to eat the life of those who look: the Kural's lover says it of one girl with wonder, 386 of women's eyes in general, likened to Siva's throat-poison and Murugan's vel.
Both liken women's eyes to poison and end with Murugan hiding his own form to follow the hunter girl; 387 takes the simile further, to the poison of the churned sea that cracked the cosmic egg.
Both stage the death-bed with wife and sons weeping before Yama comes; 376 asks for the life to be saved, 388 for knowledge to clear his troubles so that he can think of the feet.
Both set the uproar of the sects (கோலாகலச் சமயம், கலக விபரித பர சமயிகள்) against a knowledge they cannot reach: 369's reality without birth or death, 394's seal of silence.
Both make the town's talk feed the girl's love-sickness: in the Kural gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water, in 397 the town reproaches her alongside the north wind.

The song's women are அமுதம் ஊறு சொல் ஆகிய தோகையர் who call பொருளுளாரை, men of wealth, with 'என் ஆணை உன் ஆணை, my house is near'; the Kural says the இன்சொல் of women who want பொருள், not love (அன்பின் விழையார்), brings harm. The pairing shows Arunagiri dramatising the Kural's 'sweet words' as an actual street invitation sealed with an oath.

The song calls the women கரவது ஆம் மன மாதர்கள், women whose hearts hide, and the poet a fool who fell into their நீள்வலை not knowing true love (நேசமது அறியாத). Naladiyar 379 says such women hide a harmful heart (ஊறுசெய் நெஞ்சம் உள்ளடக்கி) and that those who trust their words and call them 'ours' are deceived. Both put the danger in the concealed heart behind the speech.

The song says the women's eyes are the churning-poison itself, eye-nets that take lovers' lives as sacrifice (காமுகர் உயிர்பலி கவர்வுறு ... விழிவலை). The Kural's man asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both fuse the eye with a killer, the Kural in wonder, the song in alarm.

The song pictures the deathbed with wife and fine sons weeping, hearts melting (மாதும் எழில் புதல்வரும் நின்று அழுது உளம் உருகும்), as Yama comes, and asks to think of the feet first. Tirumanthiram 157 follows the same kin, wives and children (சுற்றமும் பெண்டிரும் மக்களும்) to the town's edge, where they turn back and leave him to the fire. Together they show why the song asks for a refuge other than the weeping family.

The song has Death coming by fate's way, saying today is the day to take the life (இன்று உயிர்கொளும் நெறி இன்று என), and asks to worship the feet before (வருமுன்) that tumult of weeping kin. Naladiyar 20 says merciless Death roams looking for his people (ஆட்பார்த்து உழலும் அருளில் கூற்று), so take provisions in good time. Both press for action before Death's appointed hour; the provision in the song is worship of the feet.

The song lists the moon, the small south wind that comes like fire (எரியென வரு சிறு தென்றல்) and Kama's arrows as attackers of the girl alone on her flower bed. The Kural's woman says evening comes like strangers to a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல). Both turn the hours and breezes of love-poetry into armed assailants of the lone woman.

The song asks to enter the shade of the feet, which are a raft of lotus (சததள மலர் வார் புணை நின கழல்), out of a life worn down in the world by the body. The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). The song makes the Kural's feet into the raft (புணை) that does the swimming.

The song asks not to be born into the sea of misery by cultivating the friendship of the wicked (கருக்காரர் நட்பைப் பெருக்கு ஆசரித்துக் கலிச்சாகரத்தில் பிறவாதே). The Kural says nothing brings more affliction than bad company (தீயினத்தின் அல்லல் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). The song stretches the Kural's affliction into the next birth.

The song follows a life spent on women's breasts until the body bends, he walks coughing, speech goes (உரைபோய்) and feeling ends, and asks for the feet to escape fire-mouthed hell. Naladiyar 13 describes men whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth (சொல்தளர்ந்து கோல்ஊன்றி), yet still keep their eyes on desire, and says they have no safe way. The song is the Naladiyar's old man speaking for himself and asking for that way.

The song fears falling, a mere bubble, into the whirlpool of the sea of birth (புற்புதமாய பிறவி வாராகரச் சுழி). Naladiyar 27 calls the body a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts again and again (படுமழை மொக்குளின் பல்காலும் தோன்றிக் கெடும்). The Naladiyar's bubble is the body; the song makes each whole birth the bubble.

The song seeks the seal of silence (மோன முத்திரை) that the noisy sects cannot know, as the way out of births. Tirumanthiram 1611 says that for those to whom silence has come (மோனம் கை வந்தோர்க்கு), release and the powers come too. The Tirumanthiram states the reward the song is reaching for.

The song's women bewitch anyone at all for the love of wealth (ஆசை பொருட்டு ஆரையும் எத்தாக மயக்கிடும்) and send go-betweens to snatch money. Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison and even an oil-presser is sugar if he has wealth. Both make wealth the only thing the women see in a man.

The lovesick woman in the song says the small wind of the end (இறுதிச் சிறுகால்), the moon and the sea make her life droop (உயிர் துவள). The Kural's woman tells evening it is not evening but an hour that eats the life of the wed (உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). Both make the natural hour a devourer of the separated woman's life.

source_issues: Song 394: one corrupt character in கடலு஡டுற் (line 2), clearly கடலூடுற்; also unflagged garble தொழுத்மு டூடு (line 1), probably தொழுது மூடூடு, the ்மு for மூ seen in chapter 32.
Song 383: its last two lines are identical to song 382's (see chapter 32).
